chapters.title: What's in a Name?
chapters.summary: In this chapter: lesson 1: keeping track of cows; lesson 2: animals and their names; lesson 3: names and number names; lesson 4: puzzles with number names.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Keeping Track of Cows

activities.prompt: How could we keep track of every cow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Using Marks to Track Cows
activities.body: Deba and Deep took their cows out for grazing, or eating grass, every day. They did not know how to count. Their friend suggested making one mark for each cow leaving the gate. They struck out a mark whenever a cow came back. This system worked the next day. Later, two marks remained although no cows were outside. They found the missing cows nearby.
keyPoints: Make a mark when each cow leaves.
Strike out a mark when each cow returns.
Remaining marks help show that cows are missing.
activities.explanation: Good job listening to how the marks helped.

activities.prompt: Deba made 10 marks when cows left the gate and struck out 3 marks when cows came back. How many cows are still outside?
steps: There were 10 marks made when the cows left.
Striking out 3 marks shows that 3 cows came back.
The marks left are 10 - 3 = 7 cows.

gen.template: Deba made {a} marks when cows left the gate and struck out {b} marks when cows came back. How many cows are still outside?
steps: There were {a} marks made when the cows left.
Striking out {b} marks shows that {b} cows came back.
The marks left are {a} - {b} = {answer} cows.
gen.hint: Count the marks that were not struck out.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: Deba and Deep cannot count. How can they keep track of their cows?
steps: They used marks because they could not count.
They made a mark for each cow leaving the gate.
They struck out a mark whenever a cow came back.
Every mark was crossed out, so all their cows had returned.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did their friend suggest?
options: Make a mark for each cow.
Count the cows leaving.
Call each cow by a name.
Watch the cows from home.
activities.explanation: Their friend suggested making one mark for every cow leaving the gate.

activities.prompt: Deba and Deep knew how to count before using marks.
activities.explanation: They did not know how to count, so they used marks instead.

activities.prompt: A wall has 7 cow marks, and 3 of them have been struck out. How many marks remain on the wall?
activities.explanation: The wall has 7 marks in total. 3 marks have been struck out. The remaining marks are 7 - 3 = 4 marks.
steps: The wall has 7 marks in total.
3 marks have been struck out.
The remaining marks are 7 - 3 = 4 marks.
activities.hint: Subtract the struck-out marks from all the marks.

steps: The wall has {a} marks in total.
{b} marks have been struck out.
The remaining marks are {a} - {b} = {answer} marks.
gen.hint: Subtract the struck-out marks from all the marks.

activities.prompt: The cows made 12 marks as they went out, and 7 marks were struck out as they returned. How many cows did not come back?
activities.explanation: There are 12 outgoing marks. The 7 struck-out marks show cows that came back. The cows that did not come back are 12 - 7 = 5 cows.
steps: There are 12 outgoing marks.
The 7 struck-out marks show cows that came back.
The cows that did not come back are 12 - 7 = 5 cows.
activities.hint: Only the marks that were not struck out show missing cows.

gen.hint: Only the marks that were not struck out show missing cows.

activities.prompt: Match each action with what happened.
activities.explanation: Each cow had a mark, and that mark was struck out when it returned.

activities.prompt: At a laddoo shop, the worker made one mark for every tray of laddoos taken out and struck out a mark for every tray brought back. If 9 trays went out and 6 came back, how many tray marks remain?
activities.explanation: The worker made 9 marks for the trays taken out. 6 marks were struck out for the trays brought back. The marks that remain show 9 - 6 = 3 trays.
steps: The worker made 9 marks for the trays taken out.
6 marks were struck out for the trays brought back.
The marks that remain show 9 - 6 = 3 trays.
activities.hint: Take the returned trays away from the trays that went out.

activities.explanation: There are 14 marks for the marbles put into the bag. Taking out 6 marbles strikes out 6 marks. The marbles still in the bag are 14 - 6 = 8 marbles.
steps: There are 14 marks for the marbles put into the bag.
Taking out 6 marbles strikes out 6 marks.
The marbles still in the bag are 14 - 6 = 8 marbles.
activities.hint: Count the marks left after the marbles taken out are marked off.

activities.explanation: There are 12 marks for the children who entered. The marks for 4 leaving children were struck out. The children still in the playground are 12 - 4 = 8 children.
steps: There are 12 marks for the children who entered.
The marks for 4 leaving children were struck out.
The children still in the playground are 12 - 4 = 8 children.

activities.explanation: The worker made 11 marks for the coins taken out. 9 marks were struck out when coins were put back. The coins still missing are 11 - 9 = 2 coins.
steps: The worker made 11 marks for the coins taken out.
9 marks were struck out when coins were put back.
The coins still missing are 11 - 9 = 2 coins.
activities.hint: The remaining marks show the coins that did not come back.

activities.prompt: For a cricket practice game, one mark was made for every ball sent to the field and one mark was struck out for every ball returned. If 12 balls went out and 3 came back, how many balls are still outside?
activities.explanation: There are 12 marks for the balls sent to the field. 3 marks were struck out for the balls that returned. The balls still outside are 12 - 3 = 9 balls.
steps: There are 12 marks for the balls sent to the field.
3 marks were struck out for the balls that returned.
The balls still outside are 12 - 3 = 9 balls.
activities.hint: Subtract the returned balls from the balls sent out.

activities.prompt: Put the cow-marking events in order.
items: They follow the idea the next day
Each cow leaving gets a mark
Each returning cow has its mark struck out
They come home with every mark struck out
activities.explanation: They followed the idea, marked leaving cows, and struck out marks for returning cows.

activities.prompt: A family makes a mark for each cow leaving a gate. No marks are crossed out. What does this show?
options: No cow has come back through the gate.
Every cow has come back through the gate.
No cow left through the gate at all.
Some cows have already come back home.

why.Every cow has come back through the gate: This swaps the leaving marks with the returning marks.
It mistakes un-crossed marks for marks that were never made.
Crossed-out marks show cows that have already returned.

activities.explanation: Each un-crossed mark means that cow has not returned through the gate.

activities.prompt: A family makes marks for cows leaving. It forgets to cross out returning cows. What will the wall show?
options: Many marks will remain after all the cows return.
No marks will remain after all the cows return.
Only marks for cows that never left will remain.
Every mark will be crossed out after the cows return.

why.No marks will remain after all the cows: It assumes returning cows cross out their own marks.
why.Only marks for cows that never left will: It forgets that every leaving cow was given a mark.
why.Every mark will be crossed out after the: It assumes a return crosses out a mark without being told.

activities.explanation: Cows that returned did not have their marks crossed out.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Animals and Their Names

activities.prompt: Can we find the longest and shortest animal names together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Track Animals and Compare Names
activities.body: Hemant has 36 cows and 23 sheep. He can track his animals using marks. The teacher suggests counting large groups without numbers. Some animals and birds join a game and make two teams. The first captain has the longest name. The second has the shortest. Children can mark the shortest and longest names. They can also share their counting strategies.
keyPoints: Hemant keeps track with marks.
Captains show longest and shortest names.
Children share counting strategies.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you count animals and compare names.

activities.prompt: Hemant has 5 cows and 6 sheep. If he makes one mark for each animal, how many animal marks will he have?
steps: Hemant has 5 cows and 6 sheep.
Mark and count all the cows and sheep together: 11 animals.
5 + 6 = 11 animal marks.

gen.template: Hemant has {cows} cows and {sheep} sheep. If he makes one mark for each animal, how many animal marks will he have?
steps: Hemant has {cows} cows and {sheep} sheep.
Mark and count all the cows and sheep together: {total} animals.
{cows} + {sheep} = {answer} animal marks.
gen.hint: Make one mark for each cow and each sheep.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: Hemant had ______ cows.
activities.hint: Think about the number of cows Hemant had.
activities.explanation: Great choice! Hemant uses marks to keep track of his animals.

activities.prompt: Which animal name has the fewest letters?
options: ox
dog
tiger
elephant
activities.explanation: Ox has the fewest letters in this group. You compared each name carefully!
derived: dog has 3 letters = d + o + g
tiger has 5 letters = t + i + g + e + r
elephant has 8 letters = e + l + e + p + h + a + n + t

activities.prompt: The first team has 10 animals and the second team has 8 animals. How many more animals does the larger team have?
activities.explanation: The first team has 10 animals and the second team has 8 animals. Since 10 is greater than 8, subtract the smaller count from the larger count: 2 animals. 10 - 8 = 2 animals.
steps: The first team has 10 animals and the second team has 8 animals.
Since 10 is greater than 8, subtract the smaller count from the larger count: 2 animals.
10 - 8 = 2 animals.
activities.hint: Compare the two team counts before finding the difference.

{a} - {b} = {answer} animals.

steps: The longest name has 8 letters and the shortest name has 6 letters.

8 - 6 = 2 letters.
activities.hint: Compare the number of letters in the two names.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Names and Number Names

activities.prompt: Can you discover which letter begins the most names in your class?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Names and Number Names
activities.body: Write the names of some friends. Find the shortest and longest names. Write the starting letter of your name. Count names with the same starting letter. Find the most used starting letter and count those names. Count names with the same ending letter. Find letters that do not start any name. Number cards can make roll numbers. The number name of 43 has 10 letters.
keyPoints: Names can be compared by length.
Starting and ending letters help us group names.
Number cards can help us make roll numbers.
activities.explanation: These tasks help you study names and read number names.

activities.prompt: Teji and Jojo have friends' names on a list. How can they find the shortest and longest names?
steps: Teji and Jojo look at their friends' names.
They count letters because shortest names have the fewest letters.
They compare totals because longest names have the most letters.
They also compare starting-letter totals to find the most used letter.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Names Task
activities.prompt: What are you asked to write down?
options: your friends' names
your school timetable
your favourite games
your daily lessons
activities.explanation: The names task asks you to write down some friends' names.

activities.title: Teji's Roll Number
activities.prompt: Teji makes her roll number ______ using number cards.
activities.hint: Use the roll number made by Teji.
activities.explanation: Teji makes her roll number 43 using number cards.

activities.title: Letters in a Number Name
activities.prompt: The number name of 43 has ______ letters.
activities.hint: Think about the written number name.
activities.explanation: The number name of 43 has 10 letters.

activities.title: Shortest Names
activities.prompt: The names task includes finding the shortest names.
activities.explanation: Yes, finding the shortest names is one part of this task.

activities.title: Match the Names Tasks
activities.prompt: Match each names task to its result.
activities.explanation: Each task has a clear result connected to the names.

activities.title: Roll Numbers
activities.prompt: Teji and Jojo make roll numbers with number cards. Which statement is true?
options: Teji's roll number is 43.
Teji's roll number is 17.
Jojo's roll number is 43.
Jojo's roll number is 10.
activities.explanation: Teji makes 43, while Jojo makes 17 using number cards.

activities.prompt: Teji says counting first letters will find the shortest names. What should she do instead?
options: Count the first letter of each name again
Count the letters in each name
Count the last letter of each name
Count how many names are on the list

why.Count the first letter of each name agai: This confuses the first letter with the whole name length.
why.Count the last letter of each name: This confuses the last letter with the whole name length.
why.Count how many names are on the list: This counts how many names there are, not their lengths.

activities.explanation: Counting all letters compares the full length of each name.

activities.prompt: Children write each friend's name on a class list. How can they find the most used starting letter?
options: Choose the first letter on the list
Choose the longest name on the list
Tally each first letter and compare totals
Tally each last letter and compare totals

why.Choose the first letter on the list: The first name may not use the most common letter.
why.Choose the longest name on the list: The longest name does not show the most used starting letter.
why.Tally each last letter and compare total: This confuses ending letters with starting letters.

activities.explanation: Tallying first letters shows which starting letter is used most.

activities.prompt: Jojo is checking which names end with the same letter as his. What should he compare?
options: The number of letters in every name
The first letter of every name
The number cards under every name
The last letter of every name

why.The number of letters in every name: Name length does not show which names share an ending.
why.The first letter of every name: This confuses starting letters with ending letters.
why.The number cards under every name: Number cards cannot show the ending letter of a name.

activities.explanation: Matching last letters finds names with the same ending letter.

activities.prompt: Teji made 43 with number cards. How can she check the length of its number name?
options: Count the number cards she used
Count the first letters of the names
Count the letters in the number name
Count the friend names on the list

why.Count the number cards she used: Number cards build the number, not the words for its name.
why.Count the first letters of the names: Starting letters belong to the friends' names task.
why.Count the friend names on the list: Friend names are not the number name of 43.

activities.explanation: Counting its number-name letters checks the length asked for.

activities.title: Number Name Puzzles
activities.body: Number names can be puzzles. The number 56 is called fifty-six, and its name has 8 letters. Children look for other numbers from 1 to 99 with 8-letter names. They also find numbers with the longest names. One puzzle uses two words: 6 letters and 5 letters. Another uses 63 to 78. Venkatanarasimharajuvaripeta is an Indian place with the longest name.
keyPoints: The number 56 is called fifty-six and has 8 letters.
One number name has two words with 6 and 5 letters.
Venkatanarasimharajuvaripeta has the longest place name.

activities.title: Different ways to sort

Children look for what is common in Jojo's groups. Later, they sort pictures of household objects. They write object names into two groups. One group needs electricity. The other does not. They group the objects differently.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: how people began to count; making one hundred; writing numbers above one hundred; claps, snaps and pats.

lessons.title: How People Began to Count

activities.prompt: How did people first learn to count the things around them?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: From Marks to Numbers
activities.body: Long ago, people began counting and kept records with marks. They made marks on cave walls and tree bark. They grouped records in fives, tens, twenties and sixties. Ancient Indians made a method for writing any number. It uses ten symbols, including 0. The symbol 0 means nothing. It made the numeral system work. The method is now used everywhere in the world.
keyPoints: People made marks on cave walls and tree bark.
The number method uses ten symbols.
Zero means nothing and makes the numeral system work.
activities.explanation: Notice the early marks, the ten symbols and the important role of 0.

activities.title: Notice, Trace and Count
activities.body: Rectangles and cuboids have faces you can notice and trace. Tracing a matchbox gives three different rectangles. Tracing a wooden box gives a square and a rectangle. A cuboid can give six rectangles when all its faces are traced. You can also build rectangles with four sticks. Rectangles may have different sizes and orientations. You can count their sides, count their corners, and check which sides are equal.

Tracing a cuboid gives six rectangles.
Rectangles can vary in size and orientation.

activities.title: Count, Multiply and Share
activities.body: The shopkeeper arranges laddoos in a box. The first box is counted as three plus three plus three. This gives 3 × 3 = 9. Two boxes have 9 + 9 = 18. The laddoos can be shared among nine people. Each person gets two laddoos. Multiplication tells us about equal groups. Division tells us how to share them equally.
keyPoints: The first box has 9 laddoos.
Two boxes have 18 laddoos.
Each person gets 2 laddoos.
activities.explanation: You can count equal groups, find a total and share equally.

3 x 4 = 12 laddoos.

Two threads are used for each Rakhi.
Four beads are used for each Rakhi.
More beads are needed for ten Rakhis.

why.One friend should get all of the chocola: Giving everything to one friend leaves the other with nothing.
why.Both friends should get none of the choc: Giving neither friend chocolate does not share it.

activities.title: Guess the Number and Learn Quarters
activities.body: Clues can help you guess a hidden number. The first number is less than double of 3 and more than half of 8. The second is less than double of 4 and more than half of 10. A quarter is one equal share when a whole is shared among four people. There are four quarters in one whole. Lines can show one quarter and the remaining three quarters.
keyPoints: The first clues give two limits for each hidden number.

activities.title: Meet the Number Groups
activities.body: Numbers can be sorted into ranges. A range is a group from one number to another. School children fit 0–10, while classroom books fit 11–50. People in a bus fit 51–100, and book pages fit 101–200. Some special numbers have twin or triplet digits, such as 11 and 111. Others read the same in both directions. Teji also likes numbers that contain zeroes.

Some numbers read the same in both directions.

activities.body: Start with six blank paper slips. Write 100, 10 or 1 on each slip. Six 100-slips make six hundred. You can repeat digits when making numbers. You must arrange numbers from smaller to greater. This word system for numbers is called Bhutasankhya. Bhutasankhya means Word Numerals.

activities.explanation: These are the key ideas for making and arranging numbers.

Adding the parts gives 40 + 5 = 45.

activities.context: Many crows flew around Akbar and Birbal in the garden. Carrying rice, Akbar wanted to know their number and offered a prize for finding it. Birbal said exactly 963 crows were in the city. If there were fewer, other crows would have gone on a holiday; if there were more, crows from other places would visit. Number-line activities used 530, 540, 628, 696 and 590, and asked for 703, 721 and 759 to be located.
activities.prompt: If Akbar finds fewer than 963 crows in the city, what does Birbal's reasoning predict next?
options: The other crows would take a holiday away from the city.
Crows from other places would enter the city.
Both holiday crows and visiting crows would be present.
The city would still contain exactly 963 crows.

why.Crows from other places would enter the: More crows would mean that visitors would come to the city.
why.Both holiday crows and visiting crows wo: The two conditions do not both have to happen.

activities.prompt: How can we compare the milk in different-sized glasses and find who drank more?

activities.title: Bigger Glasses and Capacity
activities.body: Chintu says he can drink six smaller glasses. He also says he cannot drink six glasses. A bigger glass can mean fewer glasses are needed. Capacity means how much a vessel can hold. Different-sized vessels help children work out their capacity. Water can be poured between vessels to check a guess. Milk is poured into three same-sized glasses.
keyPoints: A bigger glass can mean fewer glasses are needed.
One child says she drinks more milk than the other child.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: lesson 1: the calendar game; lesson 2: comparing years; lesson 3: age and birth certificates; lesson 4: my certificate and the clock.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The Calendar Game

activities.prompt: Can we make a whole calendar from clever clues?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Missing Month
activities.body: Appa bought a new calendar, but July was missing. Amma tells Appa not to worry and says she has a solution. The children make a calendar for July 2024. They observe July and answer questions about it. They write down the July dates that are Thursdays. Thursday is one day of the week. A school closes on July 7 for 15 days.
keyPoints: July is missing from Appa's new calendar.
Amma says she has a solution.
The children make and study a July 2024 calendar.
activities.explanation: You can follow the story from the missing month to the July tasks.

activities.title: Flip the calendar

tasks.say: Show February 2024. How many days does it have?
Find the next February with 29 days after 2024.
tasks.then: Leap years come every four years: 2020, 2024, 2028.

tasks.say: Show July 2024. What day is 1 July?
tasks.then: A Monday, so the next Mondays are 8 July and 15 July.

activities.takeaway: February has 29 days only in a leap year, which comes every four years and has 366 days.
activities.explanation: February has 29 days only in a leap year, which comes every four years and has 366 days.

activities.prompt: The new calendar has no July. How can the family solve this?
steps: Appa cannot use July because it is missing from the new calendar.
Amma tells him not to worry because she has a solution.
July and January look the same, so the children can make July.
They make a July 2024 calendar and write its Thursday dates.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Find the Missing Month
activities.prompt: Which month is missing from the calendar?
options: July
January
Thursday
activities.explanation: July is missing. January and July look the same.

activities.title: Amma's Solution
activities.prompt: Amma says that she has a ______.
activities.hint: What does Amma say she has?
activities.explanation: Amma says that she has a solution.

activities.title: Match the Calendar Facts
activities.prompt: Match each person or group with what they do.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a person or group with the action in the lesson.

activities.title: Follow the Calendar Story
activities.prompt: Put the calendar events in the correct order.
items: The month of July is missing
Amma says she has a solution
The children make a calendar for July 2024
The children write the July Thursday dates
activities.explanation: The story moves from buying the calendar to writing the Thursday dates.

activities.title: What Happens Next?
activities.prompt: What do the children do after making their July 2024 calendar?
options: observe July
write January dates
close the school
buy a calendar
activities.explanation: After making the calendar, the children observe July and answer questions. They also write the July Thursday dates.

activities.title: Thursday Dates
activities.prompt: The children write the July dates that are ______.
activities.hint: What day of the week do the dates belong to?
activities.explanation: The children write the dates in July that fall on Thursdays.

activities.prompt: The family has a calendar with no July. July and January look the same. What should the family make to solve this?
options: Make a July 2024 calendar and then study its dates.
Make a January calendar and leave July empty.
Remove January because July and January look the same.
Close the school for July because July is missing.

why.Make a January calendar and leave July e: This uses January instead of the missing month, July.
why.Remove January because July and January: This thinks matching looks mean January is not needed.
why.Close the school for July because July i: This wrongly links a missing calendar month to the school closure.

activities.explanation: This is right because the children make and study a July 2024 calendar.

activities.prompt: A school closes on July 7 for 15 days. A child plans to go to school on July 7. What should the child do?
options: Stay away, because the school is closed that day.
Go as usual, because the calendar has no July.
Go as usual, because the school closes for only one day.
Stay away for July only, because the school then opens.

why.Go as usual, because the calendar has no: This wrongly thinks a missing month means the school is open.
why.Go as usual, because the school closes f: This misreads a 15-day closure as one day.
why.Stay away for July only, because the sch: This wrongly assumes the closure ends when July ends.

activities.explanation: This is right because the school is closed on July 7.

activities.prompt: The children made a July 2024 calendar. One says, 'July is missing, so we cannot learn its Thursday dates.' Why is this claim flawed?
options: The children made July and wrote its Thursday dates.
January is missing, so no month can show Thursday dates.
The school closure removed all Thursday dates.
July and January look different, so no dates can match.

why.January is missing, so no month can show: This changes the missing month from July to January.
why.The school closure removed all Thursday: This wrongly thinks a school closure can remove calendar dates.
why.July and January look different, so no d: This contradicts the fact that July and January look the same.

activities.explanation: This is right because the children made July and wrote its Thursday dates.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Comparing Years

activities.prompt: Which parts of a year stay the same, and which parts change?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Comparing Two Years
activities.body: You collect calendars from the last two years. You compare them to find what is the same and what changes. You compare month names, month lengths, days in a week, and weeks in a year. You also find months with fewer than 30 days and circle matching festival dates. You find the number of days in a year. A year has 12 months. Hetal says a year has 53 weeks.
keyPoints: Collect calendars from the last two years.
Compare what stays the same and what changes.
A year has 12 months. Hetal says it has 53 weeks.
activities.explanation: This lesson helps you compare two years carefully.

activities.prompt: Two calendars have 6 month names in common and 3 month names that are different. How many month names are compared altogether?
steps: One calendar has 6 names in common and 3 names that are different.
Adding the two groups gives 6 + 3 = 9 names.
The answer is 9 month names.

The answer is {answer} month names.
gen.hint: Count the common names and the different names.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: The children have calendars from the last two years. How can they compare months, days, weeks, and festivals?
steps: Compare the names of the months, because this shows the months in both calendars.
Compare the number of days in each month, because this finds what is the same or changes.
Compare the number of weeks in each year, because this checks Hetal's claim of 53 weeks.
Circle festivals that fall on the same date, because this shows which festivals match.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: You compare calendars to find what is the same and what ______.
activities.hint: Think about what can stay the same.
activities.explanation: Comparing calendars shows both similarities and changes.

activities.prompt: What do the children do with festivals on the same date?
options: Children circle them.
Children erase them.
Children copy them twice.
Children change their dates.
activities.explanation: The children circle festivals that fall on the same date.

activities.prompt: One month in a calendar has 28 days, and another month has 30 days. How many more days does the second month have?
activities.explanation: The two months have 28 days and 30 days. Since 30 is larger, the difference is 30 - 28 = 2 days. The answer is 2 days.
steps: The two months have 28 days and 30 days.
Since 30 is larger, the difference is 30 - 28 = 2 days.
The answer is 2 days.
activities.hint: Subtract the smaller number of days from the larger.

activities.explanation: The calendar shows 51 weeks. Hetal's number is 53 weeks, so the difference is 53 - 51 = 2 weeks. The answer is 2 weeks.
steps: The calendar shows 51 weeks.
Hetal's number is 53 weeks, so the difference is 53 - 51 = 2 weeks.
The answer is 2 weeks.

activities.prompt: The children compare two calendars. What shows whether month lengths changed?
options: The names of the months only.
The number of days in each month.

The number of months in a year.

Month names do not show whether month lengths changed.
This does not check the number of days in each month.
A year has 12 months, so this does not show month-length changes.

activities.explanation: Comparing month lengths checks whether the number of days changed.

options: Compare the names of the months only.

activities.explanation: Comparing the calendars checks how many weeks each year has.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Age and Birth Certificates

activities.prompt: Can we use a birth certificate to solve fun age mysteries?

activities.title: Bincy's Birth Details
activities.body: Bincy has a birth certificate. Her birth record is kept for 2015 in Kottayam Panchayat. She was born on the second day of May 2015. So, she will be ten years old on 2 May 2025. The lesson asks for the date of her eighth birthday. It also asks how old she will be in 2030. One question asks how many days after birth her certificate was issued.
keyPoints: Her birth record is for 2015.
Kottayam Panchayat keeps the record.
Bincy was born on 2 May 2015.
She will be ten on 2 May 2025.
activities.explanation: These details help you find Bincy's ages and dates.

The age difference is 10 years.
Her brother is 10 years old.
Hetal is 20 years old.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: My Certificate and the Clock

activities.prompt: How can a clock and a certificate tell us about someone’s special moments?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Certificates and Clock Times
activities.body: Children make their own birth certificates. A birth certificate shows the date it was made and the person's age then. They write dates in boxes for admission to Class 1 and Class 3. An analog clock or watch shows time with hands on a face. They observe the face and hand movements. Hetal's breakfast times include 7 o'clock, 07:15, eight fifteen, and eight thirty.
keyPoints: A birth certificate gives a date and an age.
Admission dates go in the given boxes.
Clock hands show the time on a clock face.
activities.explanation: This card introduces certificate details, date boxes, and clock words.

activities.prompt: A clock shows 45 minutes past 9 o'clock. How many minutes are left before the next hour?
steps: The clock shows 45 minutes past 9 o'clock.
One hour has 60 minutes, so the minutes left are 60 minus 45.
The answer is 15 minutes.

The answer is {answer} minutes.
gen.hint: Start with the 60 minutes in one hour and think about how many minutes have already passed.

Show midnight.

activities.takeaway: AM is from midnight to noon and PM from noon to midnight; a 24-hour clock counts on past 12, so 8:00 PM is 20:00.
activities.explanation: AM is from midnight to noon and PM from noon to midnight; a 24-hour clock counts on past 12, so 8:00 PM is 20:00.

activities.title: Understanding Symmetrical Malas
activities.body: Symmetry means that one exact half fits over the other half. A mala can be symmetrical when its two halves are exactly the same. Another mala is not symmetrical because its two halves are different. A symmetrical mala can use six beads of one colour and two of another. Both colours can have different bead counts.
keyPoints: One exact half must fit over the other.
Matching halves make a symmetrical mala.
Six beads and two beads can make a symmetrical mala.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you explain why a mala is symmetrical.

why.Fill the sheet with overlapping shapes a: Overlaps and gaps prevent the shapes from filling spaces.
why.Trace one path and stop after the first: Stopping after one tile does not create a repeating unit.
why.Make each tile unit different from the o: Different tile units may stop the same unit from repeating.

activities.explanation: One repeating tile unit is needed to make a tessellation.

activities.prompt: Children see different footpaths around their home. How can they use this in class?
options: Discuss their footpaths and compare them with chapter paths.
Fill gaps in every footpath before talking about them.
Join all footpath shapes into one single tile.
Repeat one footpath and avoid discussing other paths.

why.Fill gaps in every footpath before talki: Filling gaps is not the main purpose of the footpath discussion.
why.Join all footpath shapes into one single: Joining all shapes misses the children's chance to compare paths.
why.Repeat one footpath and avoid discussing: Repeating one path ignores the different footpaths children noticed.

activities.explanation: Discussion lets children share the different footpaths they have seen.

lessons.title: Finding Our Way at the Fair

activities.prompt: How can we find our way around the fair?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Fair Clues
activities.body: The giant wheel stall is near the kulfi cart. It is second from the cart and in front of the yellow-roofed stall. Puppets stay in a basket. Dada and Dadi wait for Soni and Avi in the chaupal. A map shows the chaupal, and a hut picture marks handicraft stalls. A restaurant lies right along the route. One exit is a maze; the other goes straight there.
keyPoints: The giant wheel stall is near the kulfi cart.
A map shows the chaupal.
One way out is a maze, and the other goes straight.
activities.explanation: These clues can help you find people, stalls and places at the fair.

activities.prompt: How can Soni and Avi find the giant wheel stall near the kulfi cart?
steps: Start at the kulfi cart, because the giant wheel stall is near it.
Go to the second stall, because that is the giant wheel stall.
Use the yellow-roofed stall, because the giant wheel stall is in front.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The giant wheel stall is near the kulfi cart.
activities.explanation: Yes, the giant wheel stall is near the kulfi cart.

activities.prompt: Where are the puppets kept?
options: in a basket
on the map
at the restaurant
inside the maze
activities.explanation: The puppets are kept in a basket at the stall.

activities.prompt: The giant wheel stall is the ______ stall from the kulfi cart.
activities.hint: Count outwards from the kulfi cart.
activities.explanation: The giant wheel stall is the second stall from the kulfi cart.

activities.prompt: Match each fair clue to what it shows.
pairs: the right side along the route
activities.explanation: Each clue points to a place or stall at the fair.

activities.prompt: Where is the restaurant along the route?
options: on the right
on the left
inside the maze
near the basket
activities.explanation: The restaurant is on the right along the route.

activities.prompt: The hut picture marks where the restaurant is.
activities.explanation: The hut picture marks the handicraft stalls. The restaurant is on the right along the route.

activities.prompt: Which pair shows the ways out of the fair?
options: maze and straight route
chaupal and handicraft stalls
basket and restaurant
wheel and kulfi cart
activities.explanation: One way out is a maze. The other way goes straight there.

activities.prompt: The giant wheel is the second stall from the kulfi cart. A row has 4 stalls in all, beginning with the kulfi cart. How many stalls are after the giant wheel?
activities.explanation: The kulfi cart is the first stall in the row. The giant wheel is the second stall, and the row has 4 stalls in all. The stalls after the giant wheel are 4 - 2 = 2 stalls.
steps: The kulfi cart is the first stall in the row.
The giant wheel is the second stall, and the row has 4 stalls in all.
The stalls after the giant wheel are 4 - 2 = 2 stalls.
activities.hint: Count the kulfi cart and the giant wheel first.

gen.template: The giant wheel is the second stall from the kulfi cart. A row has {n} stalls in all, beginning with the kulfi cart. How many stalls are after the giant wheel?
steps: The kulfi cart is the first stall in the row.
The giant wheel is the second stall, and the row has {n} stalls in all.
The stalls after the giant wheel are {n} - 2 = {answer} stalls.
gen.hint: Count the kulfi cart and the giant wheel first.

activities.prompt: Avi starts beside the kulfi cart and wants the giant wheel stall. Which way should he go?
options: Find the second stall in front of the yellow roof.
Find the second stall behind the yellow roof.
Find the first stall in front of the yellow roof.
Find the first stall behind the yellow roof.

why.Find the second stall behind the yellow: The stall is in front of the yellow roof, not behind it.
why.Find the first stall in front of the yel: The stall is second from the kulfi cart, not first.
why.Find the first stall behind the yellow r: It is both second from the cart and in front of the roof.

activities.explanation: It is second from the kulfi cart and in front of the yellow roof.

activities.prompt: A child sees a hut picture and says, 'Puppets are here.' What is wrong?
options: The hut marks handicraft stalls, not puppet stalls.
The hut marks puppet stalls, not handicraft stalls.
The basket marks the giant wheel stall, not the puppets.
The restaurant marks the puppet stall, not the hut.

why.The hut marks puppet stalls, not handicr: This reverses the hut and basket clues.
why.The basket marks the giant wheel stall,: The basket holds puppets; it does not mark the giant wheel stall.
why.The restaurant marks the puppet stall, n: The restaurant is along the route, not a puppet-stall marker.

activities.explanation: The hut picture marks handicraft stalls, so the child's claim is confused.

activities.context: Soni and Avi are going with their grandparents to the fair at Surajkund in Faridabad district of Haryana. At a stall, a man and a woman make malas with beads. Each mala uses eight beads, with four of one colour and four of another. The children can take beads from a basket. One mala has matching halves, while another has halves that are not the same.
activities.prompt: Soni changes a symmetrical mala so that one half no longer matches the other exactly. What should she expect?
options: It will not be symmetrical, because matching is what allows one half to fit exactly over the other.
It will stay symmetrical, because every mala still contains eight beads.
It will stay symmetrical, because the mala still has four beads of each colour.
It will become symmetrical if each half continues to use the same number of beads.

why.It will stay symmetrical, because every: Having eight beads does not make the halves match.
why.It will stay symmetrical, because the ma: Equal numbers of each colour do not guarantee matching halves.
why.It will become symmetrical if each half: Equal numbers in the halves do not guarantee that one fits over the other.

activities.explanation: An exact match between the halves is necessary for symmetry.

activities.context: Soni and Avi are going with their grandparents to the fair at Surajkund in Faridabad district of Haryana. At a stall, a man and a woman make malas with beads. Each mala uses eight beads, with four of one colour and four of another. The children can take beads from a basket. One mala has matching halves, while another has halves that are not the same.
activities.prompt: A stall worker makes a mala whose two halves are not the same. How should Soni describe it?
options: It is not symmetrical, since an exact half would not fit over the other.
It is symmetrical because both halves contain beads.
It is symmetrical because every mala has eight beads.
It is symmetrical because beads of two colours have been used.

why.It is symmetrical because both halves co: Containing beads does not make the halves exactly alike.
why.It is symmetrical because every mala has: The total number of beads does not guarantee symmetry.
why.It is symmetrical because beads of two c: Using two colours does not guarantee that the halves match.

activities.explanation: The halves are not exactly the same, so they do not match.

activities.prompt: Explain why one mala is symmetrical while the other mala is not symmetrical.
activities.answer: One mala is symmetrical because its two halves are exactly the same, so one half fits over the other. The other mala is not symmetrical because its halves are not the same. The number of beads or the colours alone do not decide symmetry; the exact match between the halves does.
points: The symmetrical mala has exactly matching halves.
One exact half fits over the other.
The other mala has different halves.
An exact match between halves determines symmetry.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Amma is making a kolam in front of a hut while children watch. They wonder whether the rangolis are all symmetrical, and they trace the designs on paper. To check, the paper is folded so one half lies exactly over the other half. Children look for symmetrical things around them, complete the given symmetrical rangolis, and draw more symmetrical rangolis in their notebooks.
activities.prompt: What should the children conclude if the folded halves do not lie exactly over each other?
options: They cannot confirm the design's symmetry with this fold.
The design is still symmetrical because folding never changes a design.
One half must be identical to the other because the paper was folded.
The design is not symmetrical in any position.

why.The design is still symmetrical because: Folding can test a design, but it cannot make unequal halves equal.
why.One half must be identical to the other: Being placed together by a fold does not automatically make the halves identical.
why.The design is not symmetrical in any pos: One unsuccessful check does not prove that the design cannot be symmetrical.

activities.explanation: A failed overlap means this fold does not establish two equal halves.

activities.context: Amma is making a kolam in front of a hut while children watch. They wonder whether the rangolis are all symmetrical, and they trace the designs on paper. To check, the paper is folded so one half lies exactly over the other half. Children look for symmetrical things around them, complete the given symmetrical rangolis, and draw more symmetrical rangolis in their notebooks.
activities.prompt: What is a suitable next step for the children after they complete the given symmetrical rangolis?
options: make additional designs with matching halves in their notebooks
draw only one half of each additional design
complete additional designs even when the halves do not match
trace nearby objects without checking their halves

why.draw only one half of each additional de: A symmetrical design needs two equal halves, not just one.
why.complete additional designs even when th: The children should check that the two halves match before calling a design symmetrical.
why.trace nearby objects without checking th: Looking around should include checking whether one half matches the other.

activities.explanation: This follows the activity of creating further symmetrical rangolis in notebooks.

activities.prompt: Explain how folding a traced rangoli helps the children check its symmetry.
activities.answer: Folding places one half directly over the other half. If they match, the design can be checked for symmetry. If they do not match, that fold does not confirm symmetry.
points: The paper is folded.
One half is placed over the other half.
Matching halves support symmetry.
Non-matching halves do not confirm symmetry.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Children make a cat mask. The paper is folded along its middle and opened before the eyes and nose are made. It is cut out and coloured, and a rubber band is tied on its back. Soni’s mask is symmetrical, but Avi’s is not, and Avi sees with only one eye. The painter gives Soni half a picture, which a mirror completes. Avi copies Soni’s counters as a mirror image and checks them with a mirror on the drawn line.
activities.prompt: The children have folded the paper along its middle. What should they do next?
options: Open the paper and then make the eyes and nose.
Cut out the mask while the paper is still folded.
Tie the rubber band before making the eyes and nose.
Colour the mask while the paper is still folded.

why.Cut out the mask while the paper is stil: The mask is opened before the eyes and nose are made.
why.Tie the rubber band before making the ey: The rubber band is tied after the mask is cut and coloured.
why.Colour the mask while the paper is still: The colouring is done after the mask is cut out.

activities.explanation: This follows the correct order of the steps.

activities.context: Children make a cat mask. The paper is folded along its middle and opened before the eyes and nose are made. It is cut out and coloured, and a rubber band is tied on its back. Soni’s mask is symmetrical, but Avi’s is not, and Avi sees with only one eye. The painter gives Soni half a picture, which a mirror completes. Avi copies Soni’s counters as a mirror image and checks them with a mirror on the drawn line.
activities.prompt: Soni has only half of the painter’s picture. What should he use to complete it?
options: A mirror, because the other half is exactly the same.
The folded paper, because folding can show the missing half.
The cat mask, because it can cover the missing part.
The rubber band, because it can mark the missing part.

why.The folded paper, because folding can sh: Folded paper does not supply the identical other half.
why.The cat mask, because it can cover the m: A cat mask does not complete the painter’s picture.
why.The rubber band, because it can mark the: A rubber band does not complete the missing half.

activities.explanation: A mirror completes the picture with the exactly matching half.

activities.prompt: How does Avi use a mirror to check the counters in the mirror game?
activities.answer: Avi copies the counters as an image of Soni’s side. He places a mirror on the drawn line so that the image can be compared with Soni’s arrangement. The counters are correctly placed as a mirror image when their positions in the mirror match Soni’s side.
points: Avi copies Soni’s side as an image.
The mirror is placed on the drawn line.
The image is compared with Soni’s arrangement.
Matching positions show correct mirror-image placement.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: How do Soni and Avi use rangometry shapes to make paths?
activities.answer: Soni and Avi join two or more rangometry shapes to make tiles, and those tiles are then traced to make paths. When the tiles form a tessellation, the shapes fill spaces without gaps or overlaps, and a repeating unit is visible in the arrangement.
points: Two or more shapes are joined.
The joined shapes make tiles.
The tiles are traced to make paths.
The arrangement uses a repeating unit without gaps or overlaps.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Soni and Avi are at the fair, where Dada and Dadi wait in the chaupal. The map shows its location. The giant wheel stall is second from the kulfi cart and in front of the yellow-roofed stall. Puppets rest in a basket at their stall. A hut picture marks the handicraft stalls. A restaurant is on the right along the route. One exit is a maze; the other goes straight. One child can guide the other with yes-or-no questions.
activities.prompt: Soni starts at the kulfi cart and wants the giant wheel stall. What should she do?
options: Stop at the first stall she sees after the cart.
Move to the next stall, using the yellow-roofed stall as the place in front of it.
Go to the stall marked by the hut picture.
Follow the restaurant to the right and choose any stall there.

why.Stop at the first stall she sees after t: This counts the first stall instead of the second.
why.Go to the stall marked by the hut pictur: The hut picture marks the handicraft stalls.
why.Follow the restaurant to the right and c: The restaurant is a landmark on the right, not the wheel stall.

activities.explanation: This uses both correct clues about the giant wheel stall.

activities.context: Soni and Avi are at the fair, where Dada and Dadi wait in the chaupal. The map shows its location. The giant wheel stall is second from the kulfi cart and in front of the yellow-roofed stall. Puppets rest in a basket at their stall. A hut picture marks the handicraft stalls. A restaurant is on the right along the route. One exit is a maze; the other goes straight. One child can guide the other with yes-or-no questions.
activities.prompt: Avi is unsure how to reach the chaupal. Which is the best way for him to get help from Soni?
options: Ask Soni a sequence of questions that she can answer with yes or no.
Ask Soni many open questions and wait for long descriptions.
Ask Soni only yes-or-no questions about which fair exit to use.
Ask Soni to choose silently between the maze and the straight route.

why.Ask Soni many open questions and wait fo: The stated way of getting help uses yes-or-no answers.
why.Ask Soni only yes-or-no questions about: Questions about an exit do not guide Avi to the chaupal.
why.Ask Soni to choose silently between the: Silent choosing cannot show which route reaches the chaupal.

activities.explanation: The other child can guide someone by answering yes or no.

activities.prompt: Explain why Soni can be sure she has found the giant wheel stall by using the two nearby stalls as clues.
activities.answer: Soni should count the giant wheel stall as the second stall from the kulfi cart. She should also check that it is in front of the yellow-roofed stall. These two clues help her confirm the correct stall and avoid choosing the first stall, the handicraft area, or the restaurant.
points: Counts from the kulfi cart
Identifies it as the second stall
Uses the yellow-roofed stall as another clue
Avoids the other stall locations
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

options: a whole picture
half a picture
a folded paper
an empty frame

activities.prompt: A mirror completes a picture when the other half is exactly the same.
activities.explanation: The mirror completes the picture because the other half is exactly the same.

activities.prompt: Which statement about rangometry shapes is true?
options: Rangometry shapes always overlap.

Every tile must use one shape.
